tagline: Hairpin turns carry the road from Republic toward the dammed Columbia.
intro: The Sherman Pass Scenic Byway takes SR 20 from Republic across the Kettle River Range toward Kettle Falls. Hairpin turns climb through Colville National Forest to the 5,575-foot pass, Washington’s highest maintained mountain crossing. Pine, fir and larch forests line the route alongside historic logging sites. State of Washington Tourism presents the scenic byway for its natural beauty and history and gives the 40-mile drive a one-hour driving time.

A dirt road between Republic and Meyers Falls served stage traffic before Camp Growden occupied a former stop in the Sherman Creek valley. Surveyors passed through the valley in 1931 as they laid out what would become Highway 20. Highway improvement and realignment in 1952–54 put sections of road across the creek or into its bed. Straightening the stream caused bank erosion, and sediment reduced Lake Sherman to a small pond. In 2009, removal of the dam’s main section and streambed restoration returned water to its former course.

Leaving Republic, SR 20 follows the Sanpoil River before turning into the mountains along O’Brien Creek. Beyond the pass, Sherman Creek leads the descent to Lake Roosevelt. The road joins US 395 to cross the Columbia and continue east into Kettle Falls.

moments.title: Republic
moments.text: Republic began as a gold-prospecting settlement, first called Eureka. Claims were staked in 1896, and the townsite was platted in April 1898. Another Washington post office already used Eureka, so the local post office took the name Republic. The town of Republic formally incorporated in May 1900. Mining brought an early boom, but processing costs shut the Republic mine and mill in 1901. The arrival of railroads in 1902 made mining profitable again, allowing ore to travel north to British Columbia for processing. Clark Avenue remains the town’s main street.

moments.title: Stonerose Fossil Site
moments.text: Leaves, insects, fish and bird feathers are preserved in the rocks at Stonerose. The fossil beds formed in an ancient lake, where volcanic ash accumulated and hardened into fine-grained sedimentary rock. Artist Wesley Wehr and Kirk Johnson, then a Seattle high school student, discovered the original site beside Highway 20 in 1977. Wehr and city council member Bert Chadick later developed the idea of a public interpretive center and fossil dig. The dig is a short walk from the center; significant finds stay with its collection. The center records the finder’s name with each retained specimen and asks researchers to credit fossil finders in publications.

moments.title: Kettle Falls
moments.text: The name Kettle Falls survived a move; the original town did not survive the reservoir. In 1940, Grand Coulee Dam flooded the old town’s Columbia River site. Planners relocated Kettle Falls to Meyers Falls, near railroad lines that supported shipping for logging, agriculture and paper industries. The present city stands on the Colville River, immediately upstream of its meeting with the Columbia. The falls for which it was named were also submerged after the dam was built. The Old Apple Warehouse, built beside the railroad by a cooperative of orchardists in 1906, remains recognizable from the highway through town.

practical: Stonerose Fossil Site: Public digging requires a permit. Visitors may keep a limited number of fossil pieces; the center retains significant finds. (checked 2026-10-11)
